issues.description: The problem text explicitly instructs students to use a StringBuilder for the Animal.name attribute, but the reference solution defines name as a String. This cross-artifact attribute type mismatch can confuse students about the expected type and how to implement getters/setters.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the expected attribute type consistent across artifacts. Either update the problem text to require a String (remove the StringBuilder requirement) or update the solution (and any templates/tests) so Animal.name is a StringBuilder and adjust the constructor, getter and setter accordingly (e.g., getName()/setName() to operate on StringBuilder or return String if desired). Ensure tests and examples reflect the chosen type.

issues.description: Within the problem statement itself there is a contradiction: the UML shows the Animal.name attribute typed as String, but the narrative text instructs students to use StringBuilder for the name attribute. This inner-document inconsistency can confuse students about the intended type.
issues.suggestedFix: Resolve the contradiction in the problem statement: either change the UML to show name: StringBuilder or remove the instruction to use StringBuilder and keep name: String. Make a single authoritative statement so students know which type to use.

issues.description: The template Farm.java declares a private method singFarmSongVerse without an Animal parameter (the parameter is commented out), while the UML and the solution implement singFarmSongVerse(Animal animal). This method parameter mismatch between template and solution/UML may confuse students about the expected signature.
issues.suggestedFix: Update the template Farm.java to declare singFarmSongVerse with the Animal parameter (e.g., private void singFarmSongVerse(Animal animal)) to match the UML and the solution, or clearly document that students should modify the signature. This ensures the template signature aligns with the expected implementation.
